enc.title: Radiative transfer: thin, thick, and the curve of growth
enc.intro: A beam with intensity $I_0$ crosses a slab of optical depth $\tau$ whose gas emits with source function $S$. The transfer equation $dI/d\tau=S-I$ gives $I(\tau)=I_0e^{-\tau}+S(1-e^{-\tau})$ for constant $S$. Sliders: $\tau$ = how many mean free paths the slab is thick; $S_0$ = what the slab itself emits (its Planck function in LTE); $I_0$ = light shining in from behind. Switch to the line view: $\tau$ then varies with frequency as a Gaussian, giving an absorption line if $S<I_0$ and an emission line if $S>I_0$.
tasks: Predict first: for $\tau=0.1$ and $\tau=10$ with $I_0=0.2$, $S_0=1$, what is $I$? (thin: $\approx I_0+(S-I_0)\tau$; thick: $\to S$.) Then check the plot.
Set $S_0=I_0$: what happens to the line in the line view and why? Then put $S_0<I_0$ and $S_0>I_0$ and name the line type.
Turn on a source slope $S_1>0$ (source gets brighter deeper in): does the emergent intensity at large $\tau$ go up or down compared with constant $S$? Predict, then check.

In the curve of growth, read the equivalent width at $\tau_0=0.1$, $10$, $10^3$ and say which regime is linear, flat, damping-like. Why does doubling the column density barely change $W$ on the flat part?

enc.title: Strömgren sphere: what if the star or the gas changes?
enc.intro: A hot star emits $Q$ ionising photons per second into hydrogen of density $n_H$. Ionisations are balanced by recombinations, $Q=\tfrac43\pi R_S^3n^2\alpha_B$, so $R_S=(3Q/4\pi\alpha_Bn^2)^{1/3}$ with $\alpha_B\approx2.6\times10^{-13}(T/10^4\,\text{K})^{-0.7}$ cm$^3$/s. $Q$ is the star's ionising luminosity (O stars much more than B), $n$ the density of the gas, $T$ only enters through $\alpha_B$. Inside $R_S$ hydrogen is ionised ($x\approx1$, an HII region emitting H$\alpha$ and free-free), outside it is neutral HI (21 cm).
tasks: Predict: $Q=10^{49}$ s$^{-1}$, $n=100$ cm$^{-3}$: $R_S$ in pc? (about 3 pc). Check, then multiply $n$ by 10 and predict the new $R_S$ ($\propto n^{-2/3}$).
If the star switches off, how long until the HII region has recombined? Read $t_{rec}=1/(n\alpha_B)$ off the info box for $n=1$ and $n=10^4$.
Compare an O5 star ($5\times10^{49}$) and a B0 star ($10^{48}$) in the same cloud: by what factor do the radii differ? Is it linear in $Q$?
Why is the edge of the sphere sharp instead of a slow fall-off? Estimate the mean free path $1/(n_{HI}\sigma)$ with $\sigma=6.3\times10^{-18}$ cm$^2$ for $n_{HI}=100$.

enc.title: Gamow peak: why fusion happens in the tail
enc.intro: Two nuclei must tunnel through the Coulomb barrier. The rate integrand is the Maxwell–Boltzmann factor $e^{-E/kT}$ (falls with energy) times the tunnelling factor $e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$ (rises with energy), $E_G=2m_rc^2(\pi\alpha Z_1Z_2)^2$. Their product is a narrow peak at $E_0=(E_G(kT)^2/4)^{1/3}$, far above $kT$. Sliders: $T$ is the gas temperature, $Z_{1,2}$ the nuclear charges, $A_{1,2}$ the mass numbers (they set the reduced mass). Start with pp: $Z=A=1$.
tasks: Predict: for the Sun's core, $T=1.5\times10^7$ K, $kT\approx1.3$ keV. Is $E_0$ below or above $kT$ and by what factor? (about 6 keV, 4.6x.)
Double $T$: how does $E_0$ scale ($\propto T^{2/3}$) and what happens to the peak height and width?
Set $Z_1=7$, $A_1=14$ (N+p, CNO). Predict: does the peak move to higher or lower energy, and is the rate more or less sensitive to $T$ than pp? Compare the exponents $\nu$.
Use $\nu\approx(E_G/4kT)^{1/3}-2/3$: at which temperature do pp and CNO give equal energy production in a star slightly hotter than the Sun, and why do massive stars burn H via CNO?

enc.title: White dwarfs: mass-radius relation and the Chandrasekhar limit
enc.intro: A white dwarf is held up by electron degeneracy pressure. For non-relativistic electrons $P\propto\rho^{5/3}$ (polytrope $n=3/2$), giving $R\propto M^{-1/3}$: more mass, smaller star. At high density the electrons become relativistic, $P\propto\rho^{4/3}$ ($n=3$), and the star can no longer be supported above $M_{Ch}\approx1.46\,(2/\mu_e)^2M_\odot$. $\mu_e$ is the mass per electron in units of $m_u$ (2 for C/O); $\rho_c$ is the central density. The curve integrates hydrostatic equilibrium with the exact degenerate-gas equation of state.
tasks: Predict: $\mu_e=2$, how does $R$ change if $M$ doubles in the non-relativistic regime? ($2^{-1/3}=0.79$.) Compare two points on the curve at low $\rho_c$.
Raise $\rho_c$ to $10^{10}$ g/cm$^3$: where is the star on the curve, what are $R$ and $M$? Why does the curve bend away from $R\propto M^{-1/3}$?
Change $\mu_e$ from 2 to 2.15 (iron): predict the ratio of Chandrasekhar masses and check $M_{Ch}$.
What if electrons were not degenerate-relativistic at all densities (no relativity)? Describe the curve and why no limit mass would exist.

enc.title: Big bang nucleosynthesis: neutron freeze-out and helium
enc.intro: While weak reactions are fast, neutrons and protons are in equilibrium: $n/p=e^{-\Delta mc^2/kT}$ with $\Delta mc^2=1.293$ MeV. When the reaction rate drops below the expansion rate $H\propto\sqrt{g_*}\,T^2$ the ratio freezes at $T_f\approx0.8$ MeV. Free neutrons then decay ($\tau_n=880$ s) until deuterium can survive photodissociation (the deuterium bottleneck, $T\approx0.07$ MeV). Nearly all remaining neutrons end up in $^4$He: $Y=2(n/p)/(1+n/p)$. Sliders: $T_f$ is the freeze-out temperature; $N_\nu$ changes $g_*$ and so $H$ and $T_f$.
tasks: Predict $n/p$ at $T_f=0.8$ MeV ($e^{-1.62}\approx0.20$) and the helium fraction without neutron decay ($Y\approx0.33$). Then turn decay on: what is $Y$ (about 0.25)?
Raise the number of neutrino species from 3 to 4: does $T_f$ go up or down, and does $Y$ increase or decrease? Check against the plot.
Delay the deuterium bottleneck by moving to a lower $T_D$ (compare with and without decay): how sensitive is $Y$ to the time of nucleosynthesis?
Switch to the $Y$ versus $T_f$ view: if weak interactions were twice as strong, would $Y$ be higher or lower? Why?
